messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 41
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Park Ranger
  trauma_type: Captivity
  pcl5: 40

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Military Topics: Talks about military, Self-Consciousness: Being seen, Authority Figures: People in uniform
  Maladaptive Strategies: Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control, Revenge Fantasies: I imagine getting revenge on the people responsible, People Pleasing: go along with whatever others want to feel safe
  Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
  Memory: Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
  Negative Appraisals: Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened, Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Arjun is a 41-year-old South Asian man who works as a park ranger in a mid-Atlantic national forest, a role he sought out, he once explained to his intake clinician, precisely because it kept him away from crowds and uniforms. He has been in a relationship for three years, though his partner has recently begun expressing concern about the emotional distance that has grown between them. Arjun presented for treatment after a routine park service briefing — attended by several officers from a neighbouring jurisdiction, all in uniform — left him unable to drive home and sitting in his truck for two hours, unable to account for the time.

Approximately four years ago, Arjun was taken captive during a hiking trip abroad. He was held for eleven days by a small armed group whose members wore military-style fatigues and conducted themselves with the rigid, performative authority of soldiers. During that time he was restrained, deprived of food as a method of control, and subjected to sustained humiliation — made to speak on command, to stand and sit on order, to demonstrate submission in front of multiple captors simultaneously. He was watched constantly. The experience of being seen, scrutinised, and assessed for compliance became as threatening as the physical deprivation itself. When he was eventually released, he was physically weakened and, as he would later describe it, "completely emptied out."

In the months that followed, Arjun found that certain moments fractured without warning into what he calls "photographs" — discrete, frozen images from the captivity, each carrying a precise sensory weight. One image is of a captor's boots at eye level. Another is of his own hands, bound. When these fragments surface, he sometimes feels a dull, spreading ache across his wrists and lower back — the body replaying what the mind cannot fully integrate. On other occasions the same memories arrive entirely stripped of feeling, as though he is reading a report about someone else. These memory intrusions are reliably activated by specific cues: conversations about military topics, the sight of a person in uniform, or the simple, ordinary experience of being looked at. A hiker pausing to ask him for directions can be enough — the sense of being seen triggers the image-sequence, and the images in turn confirm what he has come to believe about himself: that he is permanently marked by what happened, that he was uniquely foolish to have been placed in that situation, that another man — a stronger, more vigilant man — would never have been captured at all.

This appraisal of permanent humiliation and personal deficiency has not remained static. It has actively shaped how Arjun moves through his days, and in doing so it has kept the wound open. He goes along with whatever colleagues or his partner suggest, unable to assert a preference or decline a request, because compliance feels like the safest posture available — a logic that was installed during eleven days in which compliance was survival. But people-pleasing returns him, in quieter moments, to the memory of performing submission for armed men, and the self-disgust that follows re-activates the very sense of humiliation it was meant to forestall. He also controls his eating with considerable rigidity — scheduling meals, measuring portions, refusing spontaneity around food — because this is the one domain in which deprivation cannot be imposed on him again. Yet the hypervigilance required to maintain that control keeps his nervous system in a state of low-grade alert, and that alert state makes the intrusive images more accessible, not less. He has entertained detailed revenge fantasies about the men who held him, and while these briefly restore a sense of agency, they also require him to mentally re-enter the captivity, sharpening the memory's edges and intensifying the physical pain that accompanies recall.

The threat-monitoring that now governs his daily life is most visible at work. Unexpected movement — a deer breaking from undergrowth, a colleague stepping around a corner — produces a full-body startle that he cannot modulate. He cannot accept reassurance that he is safe; when his partner tells him he is home, he knows it intellectually and disbelieves it entirely. These moments of hyperarousal feed back into the memory, making each recollection feel more recent and more dangerous, and each cycle of threat and recall deepens his conviction that he is irreparably changed. He feels isolated in a way that has become structural — not merely lonely, but separated from other people by an experience he cannot translate.

What finally brought him in was not the two hours in the truck, though that frightened him. It was his partner saying, quietly, that they felt they were living with someone who was still somewhere else. Arjun wants, more than anything, to stop being watched by his own memory.
